title: What people actually look at
description: What a reviewer scans for in the first ten seconds of a portfolio, and why that reshapes what belongs above the fold.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what a time-pressed reviewer looks for first on a portfolio page
Distinguish evidence of skill from claims of skill

contentSections.body: A hiring manager has eleven browser tabs open, one per applicant, and forty minutes before her next meeting. Yours gets maybe ninety seconds before she decides whether to look closer or close the tab.

contentSections.scenario: Two homepages. Page A opens with a large photo, a headline reading 'Hi, I'm a self-taught developer on a journey to break into tech,' and three paragraphs about that journey before any project appears. Page B opens with a one-sentence line — 'I build small tools for people who track things: budgets, symptoms, habits' — followed immediately by three project cards, each with a live link and a screenshot.
contentSections.question: Which page is more likely to get a second look from someone scanning fast?

options.label: Page A — it shows personality and effort
Page B — it gets to something clickable immediately
They're equivalent — content matters more than order

feedback.a: The journey story is genuinely worth telling — just not first. Placed before any evidence of skill, it reads as three paragraphs standing between the reviewer and the thing she actually came to check.
feedback.b: Right. She doesn't need to know your journey to decide whether to click a live project. Order here isn't decoration — it's what determines whether she reads past the first screen at all.
feedback.same: Order changes what a skim-reader actually encounters. A reviewer giving a page ninety seconds reads what's first, not what's best.

contentSections.concept: The order of a page is a decision about what a reader who never scrolls will see. Put the thing you want checked first — for a portfolio, that's usually a project she can click, not a paragraph she has to read.

contentSections.body: Three things a reviewer is actually checking, roughly in this order: **can I see it working** (a live link or a video, not just a screenshot), **can I tell what it does in one sentence** (not a tech-stack list), and **does the code look like someone made intentional choices** (a README, sensible file names — not necessarily perfect code). Everything else on a portfolio page is secondary to those three.
Put something clickable first. Everything you want them to read is more convincing after they've already clicked something.

Somewhere on a lot of beginner portfolios is a section like this:

`Skills: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python, Java, C++, React, Node.js, Express, MongoDB, Git, Docker, TypeScript, SQL`

Fourteen items, no context for any of them. It's meant to reassure. It usually does the opposite.

contentSections.code:
PORTFOLIO HOMEPAGE — top to bottom:
1. Photo + name
2. 'Skills' — 14-item list, no context
3. 'About Me' — 3 paragraphs
4. Projects — 3 tutorial clones, no live links, no descriptions
5. Contact form
contentSections.question: This page is structurally sound HTML but still won't convert a fast reviewer. What's the biggest structural problem?

options.label: The skills list is too long
Nothing clickable or evidenced appears until item 4, and even then there's no live link
There's no photo caption

feedback.long: Length isn't really the problem — a fourteen-item list read in isolation, with no project behind it, would still be unconvincing at four items.
feedback.click: Right. A reviewer reaches something checkable — a project — fourth, and even then can't check it, because there's no live link. Everything above it was a claim she had to take on trust.
feedback.caption: A minor nit, not the structural one. The page could have perfect captions and still fail to show anyone anything they can verify.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Every section before 'can I click something real' is a claim, and claims are what a skim-reader is trying to skip past, not settle in to read. Move the evidence up; the claims can follow it, once she's already interested enough to want the context.

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument against ever listing your tools — it's an argument against listing them *first* and *unattached to anything*. 'React, used to build the live demo above' is a stronger sentence than 'React' sitting alone in a bulleted list, because it's now attached to something she can go check.
A skills list with nothing behind it is a claim. Attach every skill to a project it was actually used in, or leave it off.

title: A project page that explains the decisions
description: Turning a bare tech-stack list into a project page that survives the question 'why did you build it that way?'

learningObjectives.text: Convert a tech list into sentences that explain a design decision and its tradeoff
Identify the difference between naming a tool and explaining a choice

contentSections.title: Naming the choice, not just the tool

contentSections.body: Two project pages describe the same app: a small tracker that logs pain levels throughout the day. One says 'Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, localStorage.' The other says the app deliberately has no login, because someone logging pain mid-flare shouldn't have to type a password first — and that data therefore lives only in that one browser, which was an accepted tradeoff, not an oversight.

contentSections.problem: Turn this bare description into a decisions-based one: 'A recipe organizer. Built with React, Tailwind, and the Spoonacular API.'

steps.label: Ask what was chosen over what
steps.work: React was chosen over vanilla JS. Why? Because the app has several interacting views (search, saved list, detail) and React's state made that manageable at the size the project grew to.
steps.why: Naming the alternative is what turns a tool name into evidence of a decision.

steps.label: Ask what the real constraint was
steps.work: The Spoonacular API was chosen over building a recipe database from scratch, because sourcing and maintaining recipe data wasn't the skill being practiced — integrating a third-party API under a rate limit was.
steps.why: This tells a reviewer the author knows what the project was *for*, which is more convincing than a complete feature list.

steps.label: Name the tradeoff honestly
steps.work: The free tier of the API caps requests per day, so search results are cached client-side for an hour rather than re-fetched every time — a real limitation, stated plainly.
steps.why: Naming a limitation you handled deliberately reads as more competent than pretending the project has none.

steps.label: Write the final sentence
steps.work: 'Built with React because the app has three interacting views; uses the Spoonacular API rather than a custom recipe database since API integration was the skill in focus, with results cached client-side for an hour to stay under the free-tier rate limit.'
steps.why: One sentence, three decisions, one honest tradeoff — that's the whole shape a strong project description needs.

faded.problem: Now do the same for: 'A budget tracker. Built with vanilla JS and Chart.js.'

blanks.prompt: What was vanilla JS likely chosen over, and for what reason (one short phrase)?
blanks.answer: a framework, because the app is small
accept: a framework, small app doesn't need one
react, app too small to need it
blanks.why: For a single-page tool with no routing, a framework is often overhead rather than a benefit — worth saying so.

blanks.prompt: What is Chart.js doing that plain HTML/CSS couldn't (one short phrase)?
accept: rendering charts of spending over time
blanks.why: Naming *what* the library is for, not just that it's used, is what makes a tool mention useful.

blanks.prompt: Name one honest tradeoff or limitation of a vanilla-JS budget tracker with no backend.
accept: budget data is only on one device/browser
blanks.why: A reviewer trusts a page more, not less, when it names its own limits — it signals the author understands the system fully, not just the happy path.

contentSections.procedure: **Tool → alternative it was chosen over → real reason → honest tradeoff.** Run that chain for every technology on a project page before it goes live; anything you can't run it for probably shouldn't be listed as a headline decision.

contentSections.body: A tool name becomes a decision the moment you can say what it was chosen over and why. Until then, it's just a word.

contentSections.title: Writing it for your own project

contentSections.body: This is easiest to practice on a project you've already built in an earlier phase of this track — the small trackers, the API-backed tool, whatever you shipped in *Real Code* or *Shipping Fundamentals*. You already made the decisions; this lesson is just about writing them down.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the skeleton of a project-page paragraph for one of your own projects, field by field.

fields.prompt: One sentence: what does it do, for whom?
options: A generic app that does app things
A specific tool that does a specific thing for a specific kind of user
A list of the technologies used to build it
fields.correctValue: A specific tool that does a specific thing for a specific kind of user

feedback.A specific tool that does a specific thi: Right — 'for whom' is what makes it concrete instead of generic.
feedback.A generic app that does app things: Too vague to evaluate — a reviewer can't picture who'd use this or why.
feedback.A list of the technologies used to build: That's the stack, not the purpose — comes later, attached to a reason.

fields.prompt: One key technical decision and what it was chosen over.
options: Just the tool name, no comparison
The tool name plus what it replaced and why
A list of every tool used
fields.correctValue: The tool name plus what it replaced and why

feedback.The tool name plus what it replaced and: This is the sentence that does the actual convincing.
feedback.Just the tool name, no comparison: This is where most project pages stop — and where they stop being convincing.
feedback.A list of every tool used: A list reads as a claim, not a decision, no matter how long it is.

options: Omit limitations to look more finished
State one real limitation and, if relevant, what would remove it
Apologize for the project's limitations
fields.correctValue: State one real limitation and, if relevant, what would remove it

feedback.State one real limitation and, if releva: This is what signals you understand the whole system, not just the parts that worked.
feedback.Omit limitations to look more finished: A reviewer who finds the limitation themselves — and they usually do — now wonders what else was left out.
feedback.Apologize for the project's limitations: A tradeoff stated as fact reads as competence. The same fact stated as an apology reads as doubt.

contentSections.synthesis: Three sentences — what it does and for whom, one decision and its alternative, one honest tradeoff — is a complete, convincing project description. It doesn't need to be longer than that.

contentSections.body: What it does, for whom, one decision and its alternative, one honest tradeoff — that's the whole shape.

title: Writing about a project without underselling it
description: The difference between an honest claim, an oversell, and the undersell that's much more common among learners who are used to apologizing before anyone's judged the work.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish honest, checkable claims from both oversell and undersell
Rewrite an underselling project description as a specific, honest one

contentSections.body: 'It's just a small thing I threw together, nothing special.' A huge share of first project descriptions start this way — often from people who are managing a chronic illness and are used to minimizing effort in every other part of life too, so it doesn't even register as a choice. It's a habit, and it costs something real on a page whose whole job is to convince a stranger you can build things.

contentSections.scenario: A learner writes: 'Sorry this is so messy, I'm not really a programmer, but I made a small tool that tracks medication times and reminds you if you've missed a dose by more than two hours.'
contentSections.question: What's actually undermining this sentence?

options.label: The tool itself sounds too simple to be worth mentioning
The apology and self-disqualification ('sorry,' 'not really a programmer') come before any fact about what it does
It doesn't mention what language it was built in

feedback.simple: The tool isn't the problem — 'reminds you if you've missed a dose by more than two hours' is a specific, real feature. Time-based comparison logic isn't trivial for a beginner.
feedback.apology: Right. Strip the first clause and the sentence is strong: 'A tool that tracks medication times and reminds you if you've missed a dose by more than two hours.' The apology adds nothing true and actively lowers the reader's expectations before they've read the actual feature.
feedback.lang: Language is a footnote here, not the issue — the feature described is specific enough to stand on its own regardless of what it was built in.

contentSections.mechanism: Undermining language — 'sorry,' 'just,' 'nothing special,' 'not really a X' — attaches self-doubt to a sentence that would otherwise be a plain, checkable fact. It costs nothing to remove and changes how the entire sentence lands. This isn't about faking confidence you don't feel; it's about noticing that the doubt is doing no useful work in a sentence whose only job is to describe what the thing does.

contentSections.body: Reflect for a second on your own past project write-ups — the ones you've already shown someone, or considered showing someone. Where in your actual descriptions would this apply? Is there a sentence you'd write differently now?
Undermining language costs nothing to remove and changes how the whole sentence reads. It's rarely a fact about the project — it's a habit about how you talk about your own work.

contentSections.title: Honest is not the same as modest

contentSections.body: The fix for undersell is not oversell. 'Enterprise-ready' and 'nothing special' are both lies about the same project — one lies up, one lies down. The honest version sits in between, and it's usually the most specific of the three.

contentSections.scenario: A project description reads: 'A weather app that pulls live data from a public API, shows a five-day forecast, and caches the last successful response so it still shows something useful if the API is down or the user is offline.'
contentSections.question: Which of these are true about this sentence? Select all that apply.

items.label: It names a specific, checkable behavior (the offline cache)
It claims a scale of usage the project hasn't been tested at
It apologizes for or minimizes the work before describing it
It implicitly shows the author thought about a failure case (API down)

explanation.specific: Correct — 'caches the last successful response' is something a reviewer could go check by turning off their wifi.
explanation.scale: Not present. Nothing here claims it handles a volume of users or traffic — it only describes behavior.
explanation.apology: Not present. There's no 'just' or 'sorry' anywhere in the sentence — it states facts directly.
explanation.honest_limit: Correct — describing the offline-cache behavior implies the author considered what happens when the API fails, which is a real signal of care, stated as fact rather than as a boast.

contentSections.synthesis: Notice what this sentence *doesn't* do: it doesn't claim the app is production-ready, and it doesn't apologize for being small. It just states, specifically, what happens in two situations — online and offline. That specificity is what makes it convincing, and it's available at any size of project, including your smallest one.

contentSections.body: The honest version of a description is usually the most specific one, not the most modest or the most impressive one.

title: Code someone else will read
description: Cleaning a project's code enough that a stranger can follow it in a minute — without chasing a full rewrite nobody has the energy for.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a minimal, ordered cleanup pass to code before publishing it
Evaluate whether a piece of code is readable to someone who didn't write it

contentSections.body: A reviewer clicks through from your project page into the actual repo. This is the moment a lot of otherwise-strong portfolios lose someone — not because the code is wrong, but because it's unreadable in a way that has nothing to do with how well it works.

contentSections.question: What's the biggest problem for someone reading this cold?

options.label: It's too short
Nothing about the names tells you what the function does
It needs a for-loop instead of filter

feedback.short: Length isn't the issue — a short function with clear names is *easier* to read, not harder.
feedback.names: Right. `doStuff`, `d`, `x`, `i.a` — none of it says what's being filtered or why. That's the whole gap between working code and readable code.
feedback.loop: This is a style preference with no bearing on readability — filter is arguably clearer than a manual loop here.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The full explanation lives in the module's second exercise on this exact snippet — the short version is: naming carries almost all the information a fast reader gets, and this function's names carry none of it.

contentSections.body: Code that runs correctly and code that's readable to a stranger are two different bars. A portfolio needs both, and the second one is the cheaper fix.

The goal here isn't a rewrite — that costs energy you probably don't have to spend on a project you already finished. It's a fixed, five-step pass, done once, before the link goes on your portfolio page: remove secrets and stray debug output, rename the variables that would confuse a stranger, write or update the README, add a comment only where intent genuinely isn't obvious, then read it once start to finish as if you were that stranger.

The secrets step matters more than it sounds like it does. A real API key or password committed to a public repo gets found by automated scanners within minutes of the push, not eventually — this is a security step, not a polish step, and it comes first for that reason.

contentSections.question: You just pushed a repo with a real API key in a config file, then deleted it in the next commit. Is the key still exposed?
contentSections.answer: Yes — it's still readable in the repo's git history even after being deleted in a later commit. Removing it from history requires a separate step (like rewriting history or rotating the key), not just a follow-up commit.
contentSections.hint: Deleting a file in a new commit doesn't erase it from the commits before that one.

contentSections.body: Secrets, then names, then the README, then comments, then one full read-through — in that order, once, before the link goes live.

title: Three projects beat thirty
description: Why a short list of finished, explained projects outperforms a long list of tutorial clones, and how to decide what actually earns a spot.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a set of candidate projects against concrete portfolio criteria
Justify keeping a small number of projects over a larger, weaker set

contentSections.title: What a long list actually proves

contentSections.body: A learner has thirty repos: tutorial clones, half-finished experiments, one real project buried on page two. They ask which order to put them in. The real answer is: put twenty-seven of them somewhere a reviewer doesn't have to see.

contentSections.scenario: You have ninety seconds and a portfolio with thirty project links on it, no order, no descriptions.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many of those thirty links do you think an average reviewer actually clicks before deciding whether to keep looking or move on?
contentSections.explanation: Somewhere around one or two — sometimes zero, if nothing on the page tells them which one is worth their limited time. This isn't about laziness on the reviewer's part; it's the same time pressure from the first lesson in this module. A long, undifferentiated list doesn't get read more thoroughly — it gets read *less* thoroughly, because nothing on it signals where to start.

contentSections.body: The four criteria worth actually applying, from this module's own lessons: **is it finished** (not abandoned mid-build), **is it live or runnable** (a link that works, not a repo someone has to clone and configure), **does it explain a specific decision** (lesson two — not just a tech list), and **is it reasonably recent** (shows where your skill is now, not two years ago). A project that fails even one of these is actively costing you more than it's earning — a broken link is worse than no link.
Ninety seconds and thirty links means most of them are never opened. Put your energy into three that all four criteria hold up under, not thirty that most of them don't.

This is a real decision, not a hypothetical one — most learners on this track finish this phase with more than three finished-enough projects sitting in various states across the earlier phases. This pod is about actually making the cut.

contentSections.question: A project passes three of the four criteria — finished, live, reasonably recent — but has no real decision to explain. Does it make the cut?
contentSections.answer: No. All four criteria have to hold, not just a majority — a project with nothing to explain doesn't demonstrate the thing a portfolio is for, no matter how polished it is otherwise.
contentSections.hint: Think back to the CSS-animation example from the categorization drill.

contentSections.body: One honest note for a track built around variable energy: 'recent' doesn't mean 'this week.' A strong project from eight months ago, built during a period you had more capacity, still counts — the criteria are about the project's quality, not about proving you've been consistently productive since. Nobody's portfolio should be a log of how many good weeks you've had.
Finished, runnable, explains a decision, reasonably recent — a project earns its spot on all four, or it goes in the 'more projects' link at the bottom, not the front page.

title: Practice — Rewrite seven weak project descriptions
description: Seven drills on writing decisions-based, honest project descriptions and doing a minimal cleanup pass. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's rewriting and evaluation skills to unfamiliar examples at speed

contentSections.body: Nothing new here — seven drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or spread across three; nothing here is timed and the set doesn't expire.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Build your portfolio page
description: Produce a live portfolio page featuring three of your own projects, each explained in terms of the decisions behind it, with the linked code cleaned to this module's minimal standard.

learningObjectives.text: Select and justify three projects against concrete portfolio criteria
Produce a live portfolio page with decisions-based project descriptions

contentSections.body: Everything in this module was practice for this one page. It doesn't need to be fancy — a single static HTML page, or whatever you already know how to deploy from earlier phases, is entirely enough. What matters is what it says and how it's structured, not what it's built with.

contentSections.title: Your portfolio page
contentSections.brief: Someone with ninety seconds is going to look at this page and decide whether to keep looking. Build the page this module has been arguing for: something clickable first, three projects that each earn their spot, and descriptions built around decisions rather than tool names.
contentSections.deliverable: A live portfolio page with three projects, each described in one 'what it does, for whom' sentence, one key decision and its alternative, and one honest tradeoff — linking to code that's had the five-step cleanup pass from lesson four.

stages.title: Choose your three projects
stages.instructions: List every finished-ish project you have. Score each against the four criteria from lesson five: finished, live/runnable, explains a decision, reasonably recent. Keep the three strongest. If you have fewer than three that pass all four, pick your best available three and note honestly, in your own working notes, which criterion each weaker one is missing — that's useful information for what to shore up next, not a reason to fake the other three.
stages.checkpoint: You have exactly three projects, each scored against all four criteria.

stages.title: Write the decisions-based description for each
stages.instructions: For each of the three, write the three-sentence shape from lesson two: what it does and for whom, one decision and what it was chosen over, one honest tradeoff. Run the lesson-three check on each sentence: no 'just,' no 'sorry,' no unearned scale word like 'enterprise' or 'production-grade.'
stages.checkpoint: Each project has three sentences, and none of them contain undermining or inflating language.

stages.title: Clean the linked code
stages.instructions: Run the five-step pass from lesson four on all three repos: remove secrets and stray debug output, rename confusing variables, write or update each README, add comments only where genuinely needed, read each one through once as a stranger would.
stages.checkpoint: All three repos have a README, no committed secrets, and no single-letter or placeholder variable names left in the main files.

stages.title: Publish and self-check
stages.instructions: Put the page live wherever you already know how to deploy a static page. Then run the self-check below against your own finished page before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: The page is live at a real URL, and every project link on it actually works.

rubric.criterion: Something clickable appears before any bio or skills list
rubric.meets: A live project link or screenshot is visible without scrolling past personal biography or an unattached tools list.

rubric.criterion: Each project description names a decision, not just a tool
rubric.meets: Every project has at least one sentence naming what was chosen over what, and why.

rubric.criterion: No undermining or inflating language
rubric.meets: No 'just,' 'sorry,' 'nothing special,' and no unearned scale claim like 'production-grade' or 'enterprise' anywhere on the page.

rubric.criterion: Linked code passes the five-step cleanup
rubric.meets: Each repo has a README, no committed secrets, and no confusing single-letter variable names in its main files.

rubric.criterion: Only three projects, all four criteria applied honestly
rubric.meets: Exactly three projects appear, and you could defend each one's inclusion against the finished/live/decision/recent checklist out loud.

A full list of every technology you've used
A personal photo and headline

Adding the version number
Listing every other library used alongside it

'Just a small thing, nothing special'
'Handles empty input and a slow network without crashing'

questions.explanation: The third option names a specific, checkable behavior with no inflation and no apology — the honest middle between oversell and undersell.

Write the README — most reviewers read it first

options.label: A time-pressed reviewer can't check thirty links, and most of them prove less anyway
Thirty projects is against most platforms' guidelines
It's not underperforming — more is always better

questions.explanation: Reviewers give portfolios a fixed, small amount of time. A long undifferentiated list gets read less thoroughly, not more, and unmodified tutorials don't demonstrate the same thing a finished, explained project does.

questions.prompt: A project is finished, live, and recent, but has no decision to explain — it's a visual CSS demo. What should you do with it?

options.label: Include it — three out of four criteria is enough
Leave it off the front three, since it fails a real criterion
Rewrite the description to invent a decision that wasn't actually made

questions.explanation: All four criteria matter, not a passing majority — and inventing a decision that wasn't made turns an honest claim into exactly the kind of oversell this module warns against.

Is unnecessary if the project already works

questions.explanation: A reviewer trusts a description more, not less, when it states its own limits plainly — it's a signal the author has thought past the happy path, which a purely positive description can't provide.

title: Reading documentation as a skill
description: Reading docs for the one thing you need right now, rather than as a book to get through before you're allowed to start.

learningObjectives.text: Locate the relevant section of documentation for a specific task
Distinguish quickstart, guide, and reference sections by what each is for

contentSections.title: Docs are a reference, not a book

contentSections.body: A learner opens the documentation for a new library, starts at the top, and reads for forty minutes without writing a single line of code. By the time they reach the part relevant to their actual task, they've forgotten the beginning and haven't tested anything yet.

contentSections.scenario: A documentation site has these sections: Introduction (why the library exists), Quickstart (minimal working example), Guides (task-oriented, e.g. 'Persisting state,' 'Handling errors'), API Reference (every function, alphabetical), Changelog.
contentSections.question: You want to know how to make a value survive a page refresh. Which section is built to answer that question directly?

options.label: Introduction
Guides
API Reference, read alphabetically

feedback.intro: The Introduction explains why the library exists, not how to do a specific task — useful context eventually, not an answer now.
feedback.guides: Right. A Guides section is organized by task, not by API surface — 'Persisting state' is exactly the kind of heading it exists to have.
feedback.api: The reference will eventually contain the function you need, but reading it alphabetically to find one task is the slowest route there — a reference is built for lookup once you already know roughly what you're looking for.

contentSections.concept: Documentation sections have different jobs. A quickstart gets you a working example fast. Guides answer 'how do I do X.' A reference answers 'what does this exact function take' once you already know its name. Matching your question to the right section is most of the skill — most of the time isn't lost reading, it's lost reading the wrong section.

contentSections.body: A practical search habit: before reading anything, search the docs page (browser find, or the site's own search box) for the word that names your actual task — 'persist,' 'storage,' 'error,' 'auth' — rather than starting at the top. If nothing matches, *then* the guides list or a table of contents is worth skimming.
Search for your task first. Read start to finish only once searching hasn't found it.

contentSections.title: Finding the real answer inside a page

contentSections.body: A search gets you to the right page. It doesn't always get you to the right paragraph — a lot of doc pages bury the answer under three paragraphs of framing, or hide the crucial caveat in a small 'Note:' box at the very bottom.

contentSections.problem: You've found a doc page titled 'Persisting State' for a small library. It's four paragraphs of explanation, one code example, and a small note box at the end. What do you read, and in what order?

steps.label: Jump to the code example first
steps.work: Skip the explanation paragraphs on a first pass and go straight to the code block — it usually shows the actual API in use, which answers 'how do I call this' faster than prose does.
steps.why: A working code example is the highest-density answer on the page for a task-shaped question.

steps.label: Try to map the example onto your own code
steps.work: Copy the shape of the example — the function names, the order they're called in — into your own file, even before fully understanding every line.
steps.why: This tests whether you actually have what you need faster than reading further does — if it runs, you're closer to done than you think.

steps.label: Read the note box before you ship it
steps.work: Note boxes and warnings are disproportionately where the real caveats live — 'this doesn't work in private browsing,' 'this is synchronous and will block on large data' — read it before trusting the example fully.
steps.why: Skipping the fine print is how a working example in the docs becomes a broken feature in your app, on exactly the input the docs quietly warned about.

steps.label: Read the explanation paragraphs only if something's unclear
steps.work: Go back to the prose only for the specific part that didn't make sense from the example and the note — not the whole four paragraphs.
steps.why: This targets the remaining gap instead of re-reading material the code example and note already covered.

faded.problem: Now do the same for a doc page titled 'Handling Errors,' four paragraphs, one code example, one warning box reading: 'Errors here are silent by default — check the return value, not a thrown exception.'

blanks.prompt: What do you look at first (2-4 words)?
blanks.why: Same reasoning as before — highest information density for a task-shaped question.

blanks.prompt: What's the single most important fact in the warning box, in your own words?
blanks.answer: errors don't throw, you have to check the return value
accept: errors are silent, check return value
no exception thrown, check the return
blanks.why: This is exactly the kind of caveat that doesn't show up in a quick skim of the code example, and would produce a genuinely confusing bug — 'my error handling never runs' — if missed.

blanks.prompt: If your own code wraps this call in a try/catch, will it correctly catch failures? (yes/no)
blanks.why: Since errors are silent by default per the warning, a try/catch built on the (reasonable, common) assumption that failures throw will never fire — you'd need to check the return value instead.

contentSections.procedure: **Code example → note/warning boxes → prose, only for the remaining gap.** Warning boxes exist specifically because the writer knows the example alone is misleading without them — skipping them is how a working example turns into a silent bug two weeks later.

contentSections.body: The code example gets you the shape. The warning box gets you the thing that would have cost you an afternoon of debugging otherwise.

title: Learning by building the smallest real thing
description: Why rebuilding a small, familiar piece of your own work teaches a new tool faster than finishing someone else's tutorial does.

learningObjectives.text: Scope the smallest real slice of a known task for practicing a new tool
Explain why tutorial-following alone doesn't transfer to independent use

contentSections.body: Someone finishes a complete, well-made tutorial for a new framework — every step worked, the final app runs. Then they open a blank file to build something of their own and don't know where to start. Nothing about the tutorial was wrong. Something about only-tutorials was.

contentSections.scenario: A learner has completed four different framework tutorials over two months, each one finished and each one working. They still feel like they 'don't really know' any of the frameworks well enough to build something of their own.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind that feeling?

options.label: They're not talented enough for this to click yet
A tutorial hands you the decisions already made — what to build, which error to fix, what order to write things — so you never practiced making them yourself
Four tutorials just isn't enough repetition

feedback.talent: This isn't a talent problem — it's a predictable outcome of a specific practice pattern, and it happens to strong learners just as often.
feedback.decisions: Right. A tutorial's whole value is that someone already made every decision for you — which is also exactly why finishing one doesn't practice the skill of making those decisions yourself.
feedback.reps: More tutorials would mostly produce more of the same experience — the count isn't the limiting factor, the kind of practice is.

contentSections.mechanism: A tutorial removes the two hardest parts of building something: deciding what to build, and debugging it when your own step-order produces an error the tutorial's official steps never would. Skipping both of those every time is why finishing tutorials can coexist for months with genuinely not feeling ready to build independently — because the actual skill was never practiced, only observed.

contentSections.body: This doesn't mean tutorials are useless — a first tutorial for a totally unfamiliar tool is often the fastest way to see its basic shape. It means a tutorial should be the *first* thing you do with a new tool, not the *only* thing.
A tutorial teaches you what the tool looks like when it's working. Only building something of your own — and hitting your own errors — teaches you how to use it.

'Build something real' is true but not actionable on its own — the actual skill is choosing something small enough to finish in an evening, but real enough that the new tool's actual conventions get exercised, not just its 'hello world' path.

contentSections.intro: Scope a smallest-real-thing project for a stated learning goal.

fields.prompt: Learning goal: a new state-management library. What's the smallest real slice?
options: Read the entire docs site first
Rebuild the state logic for one screen of an app you already built, using the new library
Start a brand-new app using every feature the library offers
fields.correctValue: Rebuild the state logic for one screen of an app you already built, using the new library

feedback.Rebuild the state logic for one screen o: This isolates exactly what's new (the library's API) since you already know the correct behavior of the screen.
feedback.Read the entire docs site first: Delays the point where you actually find out what you don't understand.
feedback.Start a brand-new app using every featur: Too many unknowns at once — if something breaks, you won't know whether it's the library, the new app's design, or both.

fields.prompt: How do you know the slice is the right size?
options: It should take less than a full day
It's the right size if you can't tell in advance whether it will work on the first try
It should use every feature of the new tool
fields.correctValue: It's the right size if you can't tell in advance whether it will work on the first try

feedback.It's the right size if you can't tell in: This is the real test — if you already know it'll work, you're not learning anything new; if it's so big you can't finish it, you won't get to the debugging that actually teaches you.
feedback.It should take less than a full day: A useful rule of thumb, but not the actual test — a two-hour slice that teaches nothing and an eight-hour slice that teaches everything both exist.
feedback.It should use every feature of the new t: This describes a large project, which reintroduces the too-many-unknowns problem.

contentSections.synthesis: The smallest real thing isn't about time spent — it's about picking something whose correct behavior you already know, small enough to actually finish, uncertain enough that you'll genuinely have to debug it.

contentSections.body: Pick something you already know the right answer for, small enough to finish, uncertain enough that you'll actually have to debug it in the new tool.

title: Choosing what to learn and what to ignore
description: A working test for telling a genuine learning need apart from hype, and what a scattered learning plan actually costs.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a reason to learn a new tool against whether it solves a real, current problem
Identify the pattern of hype-driven, externally-triggered learning plans

contentSections.body: Two learners both start learning a new state-management library this week. One hit a genuine wall — their app's state logic has become impossible to follow. The other saw it trending on a forum. Both will spend the same hours this week. They will not retain the same amount.

contentSections.scenario: A learner is deciding whether to spend this week's limited energy learning a new testing framework.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine signals that it's worth learning right now? Select all that apply.

items.label: A bug shipped last month that a test would have caught, and it's happened twice
It's the most-mentioned testing tool in a recent online discussion
The project is growing past the point where manual checking catches regressions
Several other developers you follow use it

explanation.bug: This is a real, self-identified problem — a recurring, costly bug that a specific tool addresses directly.
explanation.trend: Mention frequency tells you the tool is popular, not that you currently need it — popularity and personal need are independent facts.
explanation.growing: This is a genuine, observable shift in the project's own needs, not an external signal — exactly the kind of trigger worth acting on.
explanation.everyone: What other people use is useful context eventually, but it isn't evidence about your project's actual current state.

contentSections.synthesis: Two of the four signals are about your own project's actual state; the other two are about the tool's popularity elsewhere. Only the first kind reliably predicts that the hours you spend learning it will be hours well spent — popularity is worth noticing, but it isn't the same fact as need.

contentSections.body: The test isn't 'is this tool good' — most trending tools are. The test is 'did I hit a wall this tool actually solves, before I heard about the tool.'

The cost of chasing every new mention isn't just 'less depth in each thing' — it's specifically that nothing gets far enough to become useful, because each switch happens before the previous tool paid off.

contentSections.code:
LEARNING LOG:
Mon: Start GraphQL tutorial
Wed: Switch to Rust (saw a post)
Fri: Start Docker course
Mon (next week): Start testing framework course, none of the previous three finished
contentSections.question: What's the core flaw in this plan?

options.label: None of these four tools are worth learning
Every switch is triggered by something external, not by hitting a wall in the learner's own work
It should have started with Docker instead of GraphQL

feedback.worth: All four are genuinely useful tools in the right context — the plan's problem isn't the tools chosen, it's what's driving the choice between them.
feedback.trigger: Right. Nothing in this log was triggered by an actual obstacle — each switch happens because something else caught attention, which produces exactly this pattern: four starts, zero finishes.
feedback.order: Reordering the same four externally-triggered switches wouldn't fix the underlying pattern — the problem is what triggers a switch, not the sequence.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A learning plan driven entirely by outside mentions will always look like this: constant starting, rare finishing, because nothing internal to the work is pulling any one tool through to the point of being useful. The fix isn't more discipline — it's switching the trigger from 'I saw a post' to 'I hit a wall.'

contentSections.body: A switch triggered by hitting a wall in your own work is worth following. A switch triggered by a post is worth noticing and setting aside until it becomes the first kind.

title: Frameworks: what they buy and what they cost
description: Weighing a framework's real benefit — usually shared state across many views — against its real cost, for the specific shape of the project in front of you.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a framework's benefits match a specific project's actual complexity
Identify the concrete costs a framework adds beyond writing code

contentSections.body: 'Should I use a framework for this' gets asked about projects of every size, and the honest answer is almost always 'depends what the project actually needs to manage,' not 'yes' or 'no' as a blanket rule.

contentSections.scenario: Two projects. Project A: a single form that collects an email address and shows a thank-you message. Project B: a dashboard with six views — inbox, calendar, contacts, settings, search, and a notification panel — all reading and updating the same underlying data as the user moves between them.
contentSections.question: Which project is a framework more likely to genuinely help, versus mostly add cost?

options.label: Project A — the simple form
Project B — the six-view dashboard
Equally, in both cases

feedback.a: A single form with one interaction has no shared-state problem for a framework to solve — the build step and learning curve are cost with no offsetting benefit here.
feedback.b: Right. Six views reading and writing the same data is exactly the complexity a framework's state model exists to manage — this is where the benefit outweighs the cost.
feedback.same: The two projects have genuinely different amounts of shared-state complexity, which is the actual variable that determines whether a framework's cost is worth paying.

contentSections.concept: A framework's real benefit is almost always about managing complexity that already exists in the project — shared state across views, frequent updates, many interacting pieces. Where that complexity isn't present yet, the framework adds a build step, a bundle size, and a learning curve with nothing to show for them.

contentSections.body: The costs are concrete, not vague: a build step between writing code and seeing it run, a larger download for anyone loading the page, and time spent learning the framework's specific conventions instead of plain language features. None of these are disqualifying — they're a price, and the question is only whether the project is buying enough with it.
A framework earns its cost when the project already has the complexity it's built to manage. It's pure cost when the project doesn't have that complexity yet.

contentSections.title: The 'what fraction do you actually use' check

contentSections.body: A second, quieter cost: most projects that adopt a large framework end up using a small fraction of its actual surface area — which is fine, but worth knowing before the decision, not after.

contentSections.scenario: A typical small-to-medium project that adopts a full-featured frontend framework.
contentSections.question: Roughly what fraction of that framework's total documented API do you think the project ends up actually using?
contentSections.explanation: Often somewhere around 10-30% — the core rendering and state pieces, plus whatever specific features the project happens to need. This isn't a criticism of the framework; a large surface area exists to cover many different projects' different needs. It's a reason not to choose a framework because of features you're unlikely to reach — choose it for the specific complexity your actual project has right now.

contentSections.body: Most projects use a fraction of what a framework offers. Adopt one for the complexity your project actually has, not for the features it might someday need.

title: Knowing when you know enough to start
description: The actual signal that you're ready to build independently, which is not confidence, completeness, or having watched one more tutorial.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish genuine preparation from tutorial-watching as avoidance
Identify the concrete signal that predicts readiness to build independently

contentSections.body: There's a specific, familiar shape to this: 'I'll start my own project once I've watched one more tutorial.' Sometimes that's true. Often the tutorial after that one gets watched too, and the actual project never starts.

contentSections.scenario: A learner has watched five tutorials on a new framework over three weeks, all different creators covering largely the same basics, and hasn't started their own project yet, citing 'I want to be more solid on the fundamentals first.'
contentSections.question: What's most likely actually happening?

options.label: The fundamentals genuinely require five separate explanations to land
Watching feels like progress and carries no risk of a visible failure, which building does
Five tutorials just isn't enough — most people need more

feedback.fund: Five different tutorials covering largely the same basics is a strong signal the fundamentals were already covered by tutorial two or three — the later ones aren't adding new understanding.
feedback.avoid: Right. Watching a tutorial can't fail in a way anyone sees. Starting your own project can — and that visible risk of failure is often exactly what 'one more tutorial' is quietly avoiding.
feedback.more: This treats tutorial count as the limiting factor, but five tutorials on largely the same basics, with no attempt to build anything in between, is a different problem than genuinely needing more exposure.

contentSections.mechanism: This isn't a character flaw — building something and having it not work is a small, real risk, and watching another tutorial is a way of feeling productive while avoiding it. Naming the pattern when it's happening is usually enough to interrupt it: ask 'would a sixth tutorial teach me something the first five didn't?'

contentSections.body: Where in your own learning would this apply? Has there been a tool you've watched several tutorials on, without starting your own version of anything?
If several tutorials on the same tool haven't added new understanding, the gap isn't more tutorials — it's the first attempt at building something.
The useful test isn't 'do I feel ready' — feelings of readiness for most learners show up *during* building, not before it. The useful test is something you can check directly.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order they actually happen for most people learning a new tool — earliest first.
steps: Watch or read one introduction to see the tool's basic shape
Build something small and broken; hit a real, specific error
Debug that specific error using the docs, now that you know exactly what to look up
Feel meaningfully more confident with the tool
contentSections.explanation: Confidence is the last item on this list for most learners, not a prerequisite for the second one. Waiting to feel ready before attempting the second step reverses an order that, for most people, only ever runs forwards — the confidence is a downstream result of the debugging, not a gate in front of it.

contentSections.body: You know enough to start when you can build something small and broken and have a rough idea where to look when it breaks — not when you feel fully confident, which usually arrives afterward.

Produce a small working project in an unfamiliar tool, plus notes on the process

contentSections.body: This lab is the whole module run for real: pick a tool, scope the smallest real slice, read only the docs you actually need, build it, and write down what you learned — including where you got stuck and how you got unstuck.

contentSections.title: Learn one new tool by building with it
contentSections.brief: Choose one tool — a library, a small framework, a CLI, anything you don't currently know — that has a genuine reason behind choosing it, per lesson three's test. Build the smallest real thing with it, per lesson two, and read its documentation for exactly what you need, per lesson one.

stages.instructions: Choose a tool. Write one sentence naming the actual problem or curiosity driving the choice, using lesson three's test — a wall you hit, not a trend you noticed. If you can't name a genuine reason, pick something else or be honest that this one's exploratory, which is a legitimate reason too as long as it's named as such.
stages.checkpoint: You have a tool and one honest sentence about why.

stages.title: Scope the smallest real slice
stages.instructions: Using lesson two's test, describe the smallest real thing you'll build — ideally something whose correct behavior you already know from a past project, rebuilt in the new tool.
stages.checkpoint: The slice is small enough to finish today and real enough that you genuinely don't know in advance whether it'll work first try.

stages.title: Read only what you need, then build
stages.instructions: Search the tool's docs for your specific task rather than reading start to finish, per lesson one. Build the slice. When you hit an error, that's expected — debug it using the specific doc page that addresses it, not by starting over from the introduction.

rubric.meets: The notes name a specific error message or broken behavior and what specifically resolved it.

title: Pull requests and asking for review
description: Writing a pull request a reviewer can actually review — a clear title, a small scope, and a description that says what changed and why.

learningObjectives.text: Write a pull request title and description that a reviewer can act on without extra questions
Evaluate why a small, scoped diff is easier to review than a large mixed one

contentSections.title: What a reviewer needs before opening the diff

contentSections.body: A reviewer opens a pull request titled 'fixed stuff.' They now have to open every changed file, read every line, and reconstruct what the change was even trying to do — before they can even start evaluating whether it does it well.

contentSections.code:
Pull request #142
Title: fixed stuff
Description: (empty)
Files changed: 14
contentSections.question: What's the single biggest problem with this pull request, as something to review?

options.label: 14 files is too many to ever review
Nothing tells the reviewer what the change is for before they read all 14 files
The title should be capitalized

feedback.count: 14 files could genuinely all belong to one coherent, scoped change — the count alone isn't disqualifying if there's context explaining why they're connected.
feedback.context: Right. With no title, no description, a reviewer has to reverse-engineer intent from the diff alone before they can even judge whether it's correct — the hardest part of reviewing shouldn't be figuring out what was attempted.
feedback.case: A cosmetic nit with zero effect on whether this PR is reviewable.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A reviewer needs two things before opening a single file: what changed (the title) and why (the description). Both are cheap to write and expensive to reconstruct from a diff alone — skipping them shifts real work from the five minutes it takes the author to write them onto every reviewer, every time.

contentSections.body: A useful title names the specific behavior fixed or added, in a sentence a reviewer could act on without opening anything: 'Fix cart total not updating when an item is removed,' not 'fix bug.' A useful description answers three things plainly: what changed, why, and how to verify it — even two or three sentences covering all three beats a wall of prose covering only one.
A title and description exist to save the reviewer from reverse-engineering your intent from the diff. Both are cheap to write and expensive to skip.

The other lever, beyond the title and description, is scope. A twelve-file, five-unrelated-changes pull request is a different reviewing task than five small ones — not just a longer version of the same task.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a good pull request description, field by field, for a change that fixes a form validation bug and updates its error message.

options: Various fixes and improvements
Fixed the email field accepting invalid addresses and updated its error message to say why
Refactored the form component
fields.correctValue: Fixed the email field accepting invalid addresses and updated its error message to say why

feedback.Fixed the email field accepting invalid: Specific and checkable — a reviewer knows exactly what to test.
feedback.Various fixes and improvements: This is the 'fixed stuff' pattern with more words — still names nothing specific.
feedback.Refactored the form component: Only true if that's actually what happened — don't describe a fix as a refactor or vice versa.

options: Because it needed fixing
Users were able to submit clearly invalid emails, and the old error message didn't say what was wrong
No reason given
fields.correctValue: Users were able to submit clearly invalid emails, and the old error message didn't say what was wrong

feedback.Users were able to submit clearly invali: This names the actual problem being solved, which helps the reviewer judge whether the fix addresses it.
feedback.Because it needed fixing: Circular — doesn't tell the reviewer anything about the actual problem.
feedback.No reason given: Leaves the reviewer to guess whether this is a real bug fix or a stylistic preference.

options: Trust that it works
Try submitting the form with 'notanemail' and confirm the new error message appears and the form is blocked
Read the code carefully
fields.correctValue: Try submitting the form with 'notanemail' and confirm the new error message appears and the form is blocked

feedback.Try submitting the form with 'notanemail: A concrete verification step a reviewer can actually run.
feedback.Trust that it works: Leaves the reviewer with no way to independently confirm the fix.
feedback.Read the code carefully: Reading the diff is expected regardless — this doesn't add anything a description should provide.

contentSections.synthesis: What, why, how to verify — three sentences, and a reviewer has everything needed to review the change without a single follow-up question.

contentSections.body: A small, scoped diff can be held in a reviewer's head completely. A large mixed one usually can't be — size changes what kind of review is even possible.

title: Receiving a critical review without flinching
description: Separating a specific, technical comment about code from a global judgment about your ability — a distinction the comment itself almost never actually makes.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish feedback about code from feedback about the self
Respond to a critical review comment in a way that engages the actual point made

contentSections.body: 'This will break with empty input.' Six words, about one function, at one moment in time. For a lot of people — especially people who've had their competence questioned in other parts of life, which describes a lot of learners on this track — those six words land as something much bigger than that.

contentSections.scenario: A learner receives the comment 'This will break if the cart is empty — you're calling .reduce() with no initial value,' and spends the next hour feeling like a fraud who shouldn't be doing this at all.
contentSections.question: Where did the leap from 'one missed edge case' to 'I shouldn't be doing this' actually come from?

options.label: The reviewer implied it, even if they didn't say it outright
The reader supplied it — the comment itself is entirely about one line of code
It's an accurate read of what a missed edge case means about someone's ability

feedback.reviewer: Read the comment again — it names exactly one thing: a missing initial value in a reduce call. There's no claim in it about general ability, however much it might feel implied.
feedback.reader: Right. The gap between 'this line has a bug' and 'I shouldn't be doing this' is entirely manufactured by the reader — the comment supplies neither the size nor the permanence that the reaction assigns to it.
feedback.accurate: A missed edge case is exactly the kind of thing review exists to catch — it's evidence the review process is working, not evidence about overall competence, which a single line of code can't actually measure.

contentSections.mechanism: This isn't about pretending feedback never stings — it can, and that's a real, physical reaction worth taking seriously, especially for someone whose body already reacts strongly to stress. It's about noticing, deliberately, that the size and permanence the feeling assigns to a comment usually didn't come from the comment itself.

contentSections.body: A practical response, in the moment: read the comment once for exactly what it says, out loud if that helps. Then ask 'what does this actually claim about the code?' — not 'what does this mean about me.' The comment about the missing initial value claims exactly one thing, and it's true, and it's fixable in one line.
A review comment is evidence about one piece of code at one point in time. The size and permanence a hard day assigns to it is supplied by the reader, not the comment.
Once the comment is read as what it actually says, the response gets much simpler — there's just a technical point to engage with, the same as any other bug report.

contentSections.title: The comment that lands hard
contentSections.opening: You open a review on your pull request. It reads: 'This will break if the cart is empty — you're calling `.reduce()` with no initial value.' It's a genuinely rough day energy-wise, and the comment stings more than it probably would on a better one.

react.situation: The comment is sitting there, unanswered, and you have to decide how to respond.
react.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Reply: 'Sorry, I'm still learning, I know this probably wasn't good enough'
choices.consequence: The reviewer now has to manage your feelings on top of the technical point they raised — and the actual fix still hasn't happened.

choices.label: Fix it quietly with no reply at all
choices.consequence: The reviewer can't tell whether you understood the issue or just guessed at a fix — and gets no confirmation the point landed.

choices.label: Reply: 'Good catch — missed the empty-cart case, adding an initial value now'
choices.consequence: Short, specific, and moves the actual work forward. The reviewer knows exactly what happened and that the point landed.

fix.situation: You push the fix. The reviewer approves within the hour.
fix.question: The PR is merged. What's the honest thing to notice about how that felt, an hour later, once the sting had faded?

choices.label: The dread beforehand was much bigger than the actual fix, which took one line and five minutes
choices.consequence: This is usually the actual pattern — the anticipation is disproportionate to the real cost of a specific, fixable comment.

choices.label: It felt like proof you're not cut out for this, even though it got fixed
choices.consequence: The fix resolving the technical issue and the feeling resolving are two different things — one doesn't automatically follow from the other without noticing it happened.

deflected.summary: The technical point still needs addressing, and now there's an extra emotional layer in the thread too.
deflected.lesson: An apology responds to a judgment the comment never made, and it doesn't actually move the fix forward — the reviewer still needs a real answer to the technical point.

unclear.summary: The bug gets fixed, but the reviewer has no way to know you understood why.
unclear.lesson: Silence avoids the short-term discomfort of replying, but it costs trust over time — a reviewer who never hears back starts writing longer, more defensive comments to compensate.

resolved.summary: The specific technical point got a specific technical response, and the fix took five minutes.
resolved.lesson: This is worth remembering the next time a comment stings: the actual cost of engaging with the point directly is almost always smaller than the dread beforehand.

unresolved.summary: The code is fixed. The feeling that produced the dread wasn't examined, so the same pattern will likely repeat on the next comment.
unresolved.lesson: Fixing the bug and examining the reaction are two separate pieces of work. Doing only the first one means the next review comment starts from the same place this one did.

contentSections.body: Engaging with the specific technical point, briefly and directly, is almost always cheaper than the dread beforehand suggests it'll be.

title: Reviewing someone else's code kindly and usefully
description: Writing review comments that name a specific problem and a specific direction, without either false harshness or empty praise.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish specific, actionable review comments from vague or harsh ones
Rewrite a vague review comment as one that names the issue and a direction

contentSections.body: 'This is kind of messy' tells the author nothing they can act on. Neither does 'This is wrong.' Both are opinions stated as verdicts, with the actual reasoning left out — which means the author either has to guess what was meant, or ask, which is exactly the back-and-forth a good comment is supposed to save everyone.

contentSections.code:
Review comment on a 40-line function that validates input, saves to a database, and sends a confirmation email:

'nit: this is kind of messy, might want to clean it up.'
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with this comment, given it's true that the function could be cleaner?

options.label: It's too short to be a real comment
It names no specific problem and no specific direction — 'messy' and 'clean it up' could mean anything
It shouldn't be labeled 'nit'

feedback.short: Length isn't the issue — a short, specific comment ('this reduce needs an initial value') can be more useful than a long vague one.
feedback.vague: Right. 'Messy' and 'clean it up' carry no information about *what's* messy or *what* clean would look like — the author is left to guess, which defeats the point of leaving a comment at all.
feedback.nit: The 'nit' label is a real, useful convention for signaling 'not blocking' — the problem here is entirely about the comment's content, not its label.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A useful comment names the specific problem (this function does three unrelated things) and a specific direction (splitting it into three smaller ones) — vague praise and vague criticism fail the same way, by giving the author nothing concrete to act on.

contentSections.body: Kindness and specificity aren't in tension — softening language ('might be worth considering,' framed as a question) can sit right alongside a very specific, concrete point. What actually reads as unkind is usually vagueness that leaves someone guessing, not specificity delivered plainly.
Name the specific problem and a specific direction. Vague praise and vague criticism both fail the author the same way — they give nothing to act on.

contentSections.title: Turning a vague comment into an actionable one

contentSections.body: This is a rewriting skill, not a personality trait — anyone can turn 'this is messy' into something specific with one extra sentence of thought about *why* it reads that way.

contentSections.problem: Rewrite: 'this variable name is bad' — on a variable named `d` holding a list of cart items.

steps.label: Name what's actually wrong
steps.work: `d` gives no hint about what it holds — could be a date, a dictionary, a delta. It happens to be the cart's items.
steps.why: Naming the specific confusion is what turns 'bad' from an opinion into a fact the author can check.

steps.label: Suggest a specific replacement
steps.work: Something like `cartItems` or `items` would tell a reader what's inside without opening the function.
steps.why: A concrete suggestion is faster for the author to act on than being left to invent their own fix from 'bad.'

steps.label: Write the comment
steps.work: '`d` doesn't hint at what it holds — since it's the cart's items, something like `cartItems` would make the rest of the function easier to follow at a glance.'
steps.why: Specific problem, specific direction, delivered plainly — no harshness needed for it to be clear.

faded.problem: Now do the same for: 'this comment is unnecessary' — on `// increment i by 1` above the line `i++`.

blanks.prompt: What's actually true about this comment (short phrase)?
blanks.answer: it restates exactly what the code already says
accept: it just repeats what i++ does
blanks.why: A comment earns its place by adding information the code doesn't already show — this one adds none.

blanks.prompt: What would be a more useful use of a comment in this spot, if one is needed at all?
blanks.answer: explaining why i is incremented here, not what
accept: explain the reason for the increment, not the mechanics
blanks.why: Comments earn their keep explaining intent or a non-obvious reason, not restating syntax anyone can read directly.

blanks.answer: this comment just restates what i++ already says — could be removed, or replaced with a note on why it's incremented here if that's not obvious
accept: remove it, or explain why not what
blanks.why: Names the specific issue (restates the obvious) and gives a specific direction (remove, or explain why instead).

contentSections.procedure: **Name what's specifically true → suggest a specific direction → deliver it plainly.** The tone can be as gentle as you like; the content has to survive being specific every time.

contentSections.body: Every vague comment has a specific comment hiding inside it. Finding it takes one more sentence of thought, and it's the sentence that actually helps the author.

title: Contributing to an open source project
description: Finding a genuinely good first issue, reading what a project actually expects, and making a small, real contribution end to end.

learningObjectives.text: Select an appropriately scoped first issue to attempt in an open source project
Sequence the real steps of a first open source contribution

contentSections.body: A learner wants to contribute to open source, finds a project they use and like, and opens the issues tab to a wall of feature requests, bug reports, and design discussions with no idea which one a total newcomer could realistically attempt.

contentSections.scenario: The same repo's issues tab has: a 'help wanted' issue asking for a full dark-mode theming system, and a 'good first issue' asking for a single README typo fix.
contentSections.question: Which is the better first attempt?

options.label: The dark-mode issue — bigger contributions matter more
The typo fix — small, scoped, explicitly labeled for newcomers
Neither — wait until you're more experienced

feedback.big: A large, ambiguous feature is a strong contribution for someone already fluent in the project's codebase — as a first attempt it risks stalling out with nothing to show, before learning the actual contribution process at all.
feedback.small: Right. The label exists specifically for this — small, scoped, low-risk, which is exactly what a first attempt needs while you're learning the process itself, not just the code.
feedback.wait: There's no experience threshold that needs meeting first — a first contribution's whole purpose is building that experience, starting from wherever you currently are.

contentSections.concept: The label 'good first issue' is a real signal maintainers put there deliberately — it means small, scoped, and unlikely to need deep project context. The goal of a first contribution isn't maximum impact, it's learning the mechanics — fork, branch, PR, review, merge — on something low-risk enough that getting it wrong costs almost nothing.

contentSections.body: What maintainers actually want from a first contribution is usually smaller than newcomers assume: something correct, scoped, and easy to review — not a big, ambitious feature that takes weeks of their review time to evaluate on top of a back-and-forth about direction they hadn't planned for.
'good first issue' is a real label, worth taking at face value. The goal of a first contribution is learning the process, not maximizing impact.

Once an issue is picked, the process itself has a fairly fixed shape most projects share, and skipping a step is the most common way a first contribution goes sideways before the code is even the problem.

It's normal for a first pull request to get review feedback rather than merge immediately — that's not a sign it went badly. A maintainer leaving specific, actionable comments on a first-time contributor's PR is often a good sign: they're treating the contribution seriously enough to review it properly.

contentSections.question: A maintainer leaves two review comments on your first-ever pull request, both specific and technical. Does this mean the contribution was rejected?
contentSections.answer: No — specific, actionable review comments on a first PR are usually a sign the maintainer is taking it seriously enough to review it properly, not a rejection.
contentSections.hint: Compare this to how you'd want a maintainer to treat a low-effort or unwanted contribution.

contentSections.body: CONTRIBUTING.md, then claim the issue, then the small scoped change, then a clear PR, then — almost always — a round of feedback to respond to.

title: Async collaboration on your own hours
description: Writing status updates and questions that are self-contained enough that nobody needs a live call to act on them — especially useful when your working hours are genuinely unpredictable.

learningObjectives.text: Write a self-contained async status update that needs no follow-up question
Identify what makes an async message require or avoid a round trip

contentSections.body: 'Working on the login stuff, will update soon' looks like communication. It isn't, quite — it costs the reader nothing to write, and it costs them a follow-up question to act on, which is the exact round trip async work exists to avoid.

contentSections.scenario: A teammate posts: 'Login form validation is done and tested. Next: connecting it to the auth API — blocked on knowing which error codes it returns, can someone confirm before I continue?'
contentSections.question: Which of these are true about this message? Select all that apply.

items.label: It states what's finished
It states what's next
It names a specific blocker and a specific question
It requires a live call to be understood

explanation.state: Correct — 'validation is done and tested' is unambiguous and checkable.
explanation.next: Correct — the next step is named specifically, not left implicit.
explanation.blocker: Correct — the blocker names exactly what's needed (error codes) and asks a precise question, not a vague 'I'm stuck.'
explanation.reply_needed: Not present — the whole point of the message is that it's fully understandable from text alone, with no call required, even if a reply is still useful to unblock the next step.

contentSections.synthesis: This is the whole shape of a self-contained update: done, next, and — when there is one — a specific, answerable blocker. Someone reading it asynchronously, hours later, in a different timezone or a different energy state, has everything they need without a single follow-up question.

contentSections.body: Done, next, and a specific blocker if there is one — that's a complete async update, and it needs no live call to be understood.

This module's last skill is specific to working at variable energy: how do you say honestly that this week's pace is uncertain, without turning a status update into a medical disclosure nobody asked for and you don't owe anyone.

contentSections.question: A teammate writes: 'Heads up, I have POTS and today's a bad symptom day, my heart rate keeps spiking when I stand, which is why I'm behind on the API work.' Is this the minimum needed to name uncertain capacity professionally?
contentSections.answer: No — the practical fact a teammate needs is just that timing is uncertain this week. The specific diagnosis and symptoms are private and not required for the message to do its job.
contentSections.hint: Compare it to what a teammate actually needs in order to plan around your update.

contentSections.body: The useful boundary: state the practical fact (uncertain timing this week) without the private reason behind it, unless you choose to share that separately and on your own terms. 'May not get back to this until later in the week, depending on how the week goes' is complete, honest, and professional — it doesn't require, and shouldn't invite, an explanation of why.
Naming uncertain capacity is a practical fact a teammate can plan around, not a disclosure you owe an explanation for. State it plainly and move on.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's writing and evaluation skills to unfamiliar examples at speed
